content: 1. The number of bacteriologically confirmed tuberculosis (TB) cases listed during the verification period should be counted and compared with the number of cases reported in the Basic Management Unit (BMU) quarterly report for the same period. Ideally, each laboratory-confirmed case in the laboratory register should be individually matched with the corresponding entry in the BMU TB register. 2. The process of matching limited identifiers from two different data sources (e.g., laboratory and BMU registers) should be evaluated in terms of the time and human resources available. In some countries, logistical challenges may prevent the identification of a laboratory register. 3. The BMU TB register, also referred to as the district TB register in some contexts, is primarily used to record data necessary for monitoring BMU performance. This includes indicators and reports on TB patients. It is also used to summarize diagnostic results and treatment decisions to ensure adherence to diagnostic and treatment guidelines. No information beyond this monitoring scope should be included in the register. 4. The TB register must include records of all patients diagnosed with TB and eligible for treatment, including those with rifampicin-resistant TB or multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB), regardless of whether treatment was initiated. All such cases are notifiable and should be included in summary case notification reports sent to higher levels of the health system. 5. The registration date in the TB register is defined as the date a patient is diagnosed with TB and deemed eligible for treatment. 6. Depending on the organization of the National TB Program (NTP), some countries may have TB registers at the health facility level (designated as BMUs) or at both the health facility and higher levels, with the latter designated as the BMU. 7. Patients transferred from one TB register to another for continued treatment are not included in the receiving unit’s quarterly and annual reports of case registrations and treatment outcomes. 8. Misdiagnosed cases, where patients initially registered as new TB cases are later found not to have TB, must be accounted for and removed from the totals (i.e., de-notified). 9. In some surveillance systems, only smear-positive cases, rather than all bacteriologically confirmed cases, are recorded in quarterly reports. Comparisons with the laboratory register should therefore be limited to smear-positive cases to ensure consistency. 10. Laboratories may serve multiple BMUs. Only cases relevant to the BMU being assessed should be counted. 11. Patients diagnosed and registered in the laboratory of one BMU may be managed and registered in another BMU. Efforts should be made to reconcile such discrepancies. 12. The number of patient treatment cards at health facilities reporting to the selected BMU during the verification period should be counted and compared with the number of cases reported in the BMU quarterly report for the same period. In some countries, TB patients retain their treatment cards, making this assessment infeasible. 13. In countries where the BMU is at the district level with multiple health facilities reporting to it, each health facility may maintain its own TB register. In such cases, the combined totals from all health facility TB registers reporting to the BMU should be compared with the BMU TB register and quarterly report for the same verification period. 14. The BMU TB register should match the BMU quarterly report. For the third benchmark, a BMU is considered acceptable if at least 95% of TB cases have complete data for all variables in the minimum dataset. 15. When benchmarks are not met, corrective actions such as monitoring and evaluation (M&E) training, increased supervision frequency, and improved supervision quality should be implemented. 16. Paper-based systems often present challenges in data quality assessment. Countries should consider transitioning to electronic recording and reporting systems to improve data accuracy and completeness. 17. National guidelines for recording and reporting data may need to be updated to reflect the benchmarks. Key actions to address gaps in meeting the benchmarks should be described, along with an estimated budget to support these activities. 18. Data quality issues such as missing values, invalid or unclear values, and inconsistencies should be minimized. Electronic systems can help prevent these issues through automated validation checks during data entry and subsequent database queries. 19. Missing values occur when essential information about a TB case, such as date of birth or age, is not recorded. Mandatory fields during data entry can help prevent this, but a balance between stringency and practicality is necessary. 20. Invalid or unclear values often arise in free-text fields. Structured data entry methods, such as drop-down lists or tick boxes, can reduce these errors. 21. Inconsistent or misclassified values occur when recorded facts about a case contradict each other. Examples include mismatched age and date of birth, incorrect sex classification, or contradictory treatment history. These errors can be minimized through electronic systems and active use by knowledgeable staff. 22. Data quality assessments should ensure that ≥90% of case records are complete, valid, and internally consistent, with <1% unresolved duplicates in the national dataset. Reliable data is essential for accurate measurement of TB incidence and program performance.
